outcome: I can explain how changes in the determinants of demand and supply shift the curves, how the price mechanism moves the market to a new equilibrium, and the difference between a shift and a movement along a curve.

learn.text:
[[Demand]] is the quantity of a good that buyers are willing and able to buy at each price. [[Supply]] is the quantity that firms are willing and able to sell at each price. Where the two curves cross, the market is in [[equilibrium]]: quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.

A change in the good's own price causes a [[movement along the curve]]. A change in anything else, a [[non-price determinant of demand|non-price determinants of demand]] or a [[non-price determinant of supply|non-price determinants of supply]], causes a [[shift of the curve]]. We assume everything else stays the same: [[ceteris paribus]].

After a shift, the old price no longer clears the market. There is [[excess demand]] (a shortage) or [[excess supply]] (a surplus). The [[price mechanism]] fixes this: the price changes, which works as a [[signal|signalling]], an [[incentive]] and a way of [[rationing]] scarce goods, until the market reaches a new equilibrium.
learn.caption: Demand shifts right from D₁ to D₂. The equilibrium moves from P₁ and Q₁ to P₂ and Q₂: price rises and quantity rises.

try.intro:
**Welcome to Riverton**. You run the market for **bags of roasted coffee beans**. Every scenario starts from the same market, at $5 and 50 bags (ceteris paribus).

1. Read the event scenario and **predict**: which curve shifts, and which way?
2. **Drag the curve** on the diagram.
3. Watch the shortage or surplus at the old price, then let the price adjust.
4. Say which function of the price mechanism the scenario shows.

There are three levels. Each opens when you earn the stamp for the level before.
try.marketName: Market for coffee beans in Riverton

options.text: Demand shifts left
Demand shifts right
Supply shifts left
Supply shifts right
No shift: a movement along a curve

demand.text: No shift: a movement along the demand curve

supply.text: No shift: a movement along the supply curve

feedback.wrong-direction: Good start: you picked the right curve. Check the direction. Ask: at every price, do people now want to buy (or firms want to sell) more or less than before?
feedback.wrong-curve: Good thinking, but it is the other curve. Ask: does this event change what **buyers** want (demand) or what **sellers** can or want to sell (supply)?
feedback.missed-shift: This one does shift a curve. Something other than the coffee's own price changed, so it is a non-price determinant. Ask: is it a determinant of demand or of supply?
feedback.movement-not-shift: This is the trap! Only the coffee's own price changed (or the other curve moved). A change in a good's own price causes a **movement along** the curve, not a shift.

mechanismInfo.signalling: **Signalling**: a price change sends information. It shows buyers and sellers where resources are wanted and where they are not.
mechanismInfo.incentive: **Incentive**: a price change gives buyers and sellers a reason to change what they do. For example, a higher price means more profit, so firms produce more.
mechanismInfo.rationing: **Rationing**: price decides who gets a scarce good. When price rises, only buyers willing and able to pay the higher price still buy.

hlQuestion.prompt: **HL challenge.** In the trap scenarios, a lower coffee price makes quantity demanded rise. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: Roasters want to sell more at a lower price
options.feedback: That is about sellers, and it is the wrong way round: the law of supply says firms sell **less** at a lower price.

options.text: Each extra bag gives more satisfaction than the one before
options.feedback: It is the other way round. The law of diminishing marginal utility says each extra unit gives **less** extra satisfaction.

options.text: Coffee is now cheaper than tea, so some people switch to coffee, and their income now buys more
options.feedback: Yes. These are the **substitution effect** (coffee is cheaper compared with substitutes) and the **income effect** (the same income buys more). Diminishing marginal utility also helps: each extra bag gives less extra satisfaction, so people buy more only when the price falls.

options.text: The lower price shifts the demand curve to the right
options.feedback: A change in the good's own price never shifts its demand curve. It causes a movement along it.

cards.title: Pay rise in Riverton
cards.text: Most workers in Riverton get a 10% pay rise. Coffee beans are a **normal good**.
cards.explain: Coffee beans are a [[normal good]], so higher income means people want to buy more at every price. Demand shifts right from D₁ to D₂.

mechanism.sentence: The higher price tells roasters that buyers now want more coffee beans.

cards.title: Pay rise, goodbye instant coffee
cards.market: In this scenario the market is **store-brand instant coffee**, an **inferior good** in Riverton.
cards.text: Incomes rise across Riverton. Many people stop buying cheap instant coffee and buy better beans instead.
cards.explain: For an [[inferior good]], higher income means people buy **less** at every price. Demand for instant coffee shifts left from D₁ to D₂.

mechanism.sentence: The lower price of instant coffee tells its makers that buyers want less of it, so resources can move to other goods.

cards.title: Health study
cards.text: A popular health study says two cups of coffee a day are good for you. People in Riverton want more coffee.
cards.explain: A change in tastes and preferences in favour of coffee raises the quantity people want at every price. Demand shifts right.

mechanism.sentence: As the price rises, some buyers decide coffee is no longer worth it, so the limited beans go to the buyers who value them most.

cards.title: Sleep worries
cards.text: A viral video says coffee ruins your sleep. Many people in Riverton decide to drink less coffee.
cards.explain: Tastes and preferences move away from coffee, so people want less at every price. Demand shifts left.

mechanism.sentence: The lower price means roasting coffee earns less profit, so some roasters roast fewer beans.

cards.title: Stock up now!
cards.text: News reports say coffee prices will rise next month. Shoppers buy extra bags today to beat the price rise.
cards.explain: When buyers expect a higher price in the future, they buy more **now**. Demand today shifts right.

mechanism.sentence: The higher price makes roasting more profitable, so roasters add extra shifts.

cards.title: Cheap tea
cards.text: A huge tea harvest makes tea much cheaper in Riverton. Tea and coffee are [[substitutes]].
cards.explain: Tea is a substitute for coffee. When tea becomes cheaper, some people switch from coffee to tea, so demand for coffee shifts left at every price.

mechanism.sentence: The falling coffee price shows roasters that buyers want less coffee than before.

cards.title: Coffee machine sale
cards.text: The price of home coffee machines falls by half. Coffee machines and coffee beans are [[complements]].
cards.explain: Coffee machines and beans are used together. Cheaper machines mean more people make coffee at home, so demand for beans shifts right.

mechanism.sentence: At the higher price, only buyers who are willing and able to pay it get the coffee beans.

cards.title: New university
cards.text: A new university opens in Riverton. 5,000 students move to the city, and many of them drink coffee.
cards.explain: More consumers in the market means more coffee is wanted at every price. Demand shifts right.

mechanism.sentence: Roasters see a chance of higher profit, so they roast more beans.

cards.determinant: Supply: costs of factors of production
cards.title: Frost on the farms
cards.text: A frost damages coffee farms abroad. Green coffee beans, the roasters' main raw material, now cost much more.
cards.explain: Higher costs of [[factors of production]] (here, raw materials) make roasting each bag more costly. Roasters supply less at every price. Supply shifts left.

mechanism.sentence: With fewer beans for sale, the higher price makes some buyers cut back, so the scarce beans go to those most willing to pay.

cards.determinant: Supply: costs of factors of production
cards.title: Higher wages
cards.text: Workers at Riverton's roasteries win a higher wage. Each bag now costs more to make.
cards.explain: Wages are the cost of labour, a factor of production. Higher costs mean firms supply less at every price. Supply shifts left.

mechanism.sentence: The higher price tells everyone in the market that coffee beans have become scarcer.

cards.title: Coffee tax
cards.text: The government puts an [[indirect tax]] of $1 on every bag of coffee beans sold.
cards.explain: An indirect tax is like an extra cost for firms on each unit. They supply less at every price, so supply shifts left (up by the tax).

mechanism.sentence: Buyers who value coffee less than the new, higher price stop buying it.

cards.title: Roaster subsidy
cards.text: The government pays roasters a [[subsidy]] of $1 for every bag they sell.
cards.explain: A subsidy lowers firms' costs, so they supply more at every price. Supply shifts right (down by the subsidy).

mechanism.sentence: The lower price gives buyers a reason to buy more coffee beans.

cards.title: Faster roasters
cards.text: A new roasting machine roasts twice as many beans per hour with the same workers.
cards.explain: Better technology lowers the cost of making each bag. Firms supply more at every price. Supply shifts right.

mechanism.sentence: The lower price tells buyers that coffee beans are now more plentiful.

cards.title: New roasteries
cards.text: Three new roasteries open in Riverton.
cards.explain: More firms in the market means more coffee is offered at every price. Supply shifts right.

mechanism.sentence: The lower price encourages bakeries to use more coffee in their cakes.

cards.title: Holding stock
cards.text: Roasters expect coffee prices to be much higher next month. They keep some bags in storage to sell later.
cards.explain: When firms expect a higher price in the future, they offer less for sale **now**. Supply today shifts left.

mechanism.sentence: Fewer bags are on the shelves today, and the higher price decides which buyers get them.

cards.determinant: Supply: price of a good in joint supply
cards.title: Caffeine boom
cards.market: In this scenario the market is **decaf coffee beans**.
cards.text: Energy drink makers pay much more for caffeine. Taking the caffeine out of coffee beans makes two products at once: caffeine and decaf beans.
cards.explain: Caffeine and decaf beans are in [[joint supply]]: making one also makes the other. The higher price of caffeine makes firms decaffeinate more beans, so the supply of decaf beans shifts right.

mechanism.sentence: The falling price of decaf beans tells decaf buyers that more is now available.

cards.determinant: Supply: price of a good in competitive supply
cards.title: Cocoa price jumps
cards.market: In this scenario the market is **green coffee beans from Riverton's hill farms**.
cards.text: The price of cocoa rises sharply. Hill farmers can grow coffee or cocoa on the same land.
cards.explain: Coffee and cocoa are in [[competitive supply]]: they compete for the same land. Cocoa is now more profitable, so farmers grow more cocoa and less coffee. Supply of coffee shifts left.

mechanism.sentence: Farmers moved land to cocoa because the higher cocoa price meant more profit.

traps.title: Roasters raise prices
traps.text: Roasters raise the price of a bag from $5 to $7. Nothing else changes.
traps.question: What happens to the **demand curve** for coffee beans?
traps.explain: Only the coffee's own price changed. Buyers move **up along** D₁: quantity demanded falls from 50 to 30 bags. The demand curve does not shift.

traps.title: Big coffee sale
traps.text: Roasters cut the price of a bag from $5 to $3 for a sale. Nothing else changes.
traps.question: What happens to the **demand curve** for coffee beans?
traps.explain: Only the coffee's own price changed. Buyers move **down along** D₁: quantity demanded rises from 50 to 70 bags. The demand curve does not shift. ^HL^ Why do people buy more? Try the HL challenge below.

traps.title: Better price for roasters
traps.text: The price of a bag rises from $5 to $7, so roasters offer more bags for sale.
traps.question: What happens to the **supply curve** of coffee beans?
traps.explain: Only the coffee's own price changed. Roasters move **up along** S₁: quantity supplied rises from 50 to 70 bags. The supply curve does not shift.

traps.title: Frost again
traps.text: A frost cuts the supply of coffee beans, and the price of coffee rises.
traps.question: What happens to the **demand curve** for coffee beans?
traps.explain: Supply shifted left, not demand. The higher price makes buyers move **up along** the demand curve D, so quantity demanded falls. Demand only shifts when a non-price determinant of demand changes, and none did.

traps.title: Students arrive
traps.text: A new university brings thousands of coffee drinkers to Riverton, and the price of coffee rises.
traps.question: What happens to the **supply curve** of coffee beans?
traps.explain: Demand shifted right, not supply. The higher price gives roasters an incentive to sell more, so they move **up along** the supply curve S. Supply only shifts when a non-price determinant of supply changes, and none did.

levels.title: Single shifts
levels.blurb: One curve shifts in each scenario. Get 6 of 8 right.

levels.title: Shift or movement?
levels.blurb: Trap scenarios, shifts of different sizes, and you predict the new price and quantity. Get 6 of 8 right.

levels.title: Double shocks
levels.blurb: Two events hit the market at once. Predict both shifts, then price and quantity. Get 4 of 6 right.

try.goal: Read each scenario and predict how the market reacts. Get 6 of 8 right to earn the **Market Mover** stamp.

check.prompt: A bakery raises the price of its croissants. Nothing else changes. What happens in the market for the bakery's croissants?

options.text: The supply curve shifts left
options.feedback: The bakery's costs and technology did not change, so supply does not shift. The price change is a movement along the curves.

options.text: A movement up along the demand curve: quantity demanded falls
options.feedback: Yes. A change in the good's own price causes a movement along the demand curve, not a shift.

options.text: The demand curve shifts left
options.feedback: A shift needs a change in a non-price determinant, such as income or tastes. Here only the croissant's own price changed.

options.text: The demand curve shifts right
options.feedback: A higher price does not make people want more at every price. And a change in the good's own price never shifts its demand curve.

hints: Is the thing that changed the good's own price, or something else?
A change in the good's own price moves you along a curve. A change in anything else shifts it.
check.worked: Example: a cinema raises the price of a film from $10 to $12. Fewer people buy seats. On the diagram we move up along the same demand curve, from one point to another. The curve stays where it is.
check.explanation: Demand shows the quantity bought at **every** price. When only the price changes, we read a different point on the same curve: a movement along it, called a change in quantity demanded.

check.prompt: The price of tea rises. Tea and coffee are substitutes. What happens to the equilibrium in the **coffee** market?

options.text: Supply of coffee shifts left: price rises and quantity falls
options.feedback: The price of tea affects coffee buyers, not coffee sellers' costs. So it is a demand change.

options.text: Movement along the coffee demand curve, no shift
options.feedback: The price of a **related good** changed, not the price of coffee itself. That is a non-price determinant, so the coffee demand curve shifts.

options.text: Demand for coffee shifts right: price rises and quantity rises
options.feedback: Yes. Some tea drinkers switch to coffee, so demand for coffee rises at every price.

options.text: Demand for coffee shifts left: price falls and quantity falls
options.feedback: That would happen if tea became **cheaper**. Dearer tea pushes people towards coffee.

hints: Does this change affect coffee buyers or coffee sellers?
If tea is dearer, what do some tea drinkers do instead?
check.worked: Example: bus fares rise. Bus and train travel are substitutes. Some people switch to the train, so demand for train travel shifts right. Train fares and the number of train trips both rise.
check.explanation: For substitutes, a higher price of one good raises demand for the other. Demand for coffee shifts right, so the equilibrium price and quantity of coffee both rise.

check.prompt: The government puts an indirect tax on each bottle of juice sold. What happens in the juice market?

options.text: Demand shifts left: price falls and quantity falls
options.feedback: The tax is paid by firms to the government, so it changes their costs: a supply change. Buyers' tastes and incomes did not change.

options.text: Supply shifts right: price falls and quantity rises
options.feedback: That is what a **subsidy** does. A tax raises firms' costs, so supply shifts the other way.

options.text: Nothing changes, because the tax is paid by firms
options.feedback: Firms supply less when their costs rise. That changes the market equilibrium.

options.text: Supply shifts left: price rises and quantity falls
options.feedback: Yes. The tax acts like a higher cost per bottle, so firms supply less at every price.

hints: Who pays the tax to the government, buyers or firms?
A tax per unit works like an extra cost of production.
check.worked: Example: wages for drivers rise. Each taxi ride now costs more to provide, so taxi firms offer fewer rides at every price. Supply shifts left: fares rise and fewer rides are taken.
check.explanation: An [[indirect tax]] raises the cost of supplying each unit. Supply shifts left (up by the tax), so equilibrium price rises and equilibrium quantity falls.

check.prompt: Concert seats are scarce. "Because the price is high, only fans who are willing and able to pay it get seats." Which function of the price mechanism does this sentence describe?

options.text: Allocative efficiency
options.feedback: Allocative efficiency is a result of a working market, not one of the three functions of the price mechanism.

options.text: Rationing
options.feedback: Yes. The price decides who gets the scarce good.

options.text: Signalling
options.feedback: Signalling is about the **information** a price change sends to buyers and sellers. This sentence is about who gets the seats.

options.text: Incentive
options.feedback: Incentive is about price giving people a **reason to change** what they do, such as making more. This sentence is about sharing out a scarce good.

hints: The three functions are signalling, incentive and rationing.
The sentence is about **who gets** the good.
check.worked: Example: "A higher price for avocados tells farmers that buyers want more avocados." This is about information, so it is signalling. "The higher price makes avocado farming more profitable, so farmers plant more trees." That is incentive.
check.explanation: Rationing means price shares out scarce goods. When price is high, only buyers who are willing and able to pay it buy. Others drop out.

check.prompt: Two things happen at once in the market for bicycles: incomes rise (bicycles are a normal good), and a new technology makes bicycles cheaper to build. What can we say for sure about the new equilibrium?

options.text: Price falls and quantity rises
options.feedback: This happens only if the supply shift is bigger than the demand shift. We are not told the sizes.

options.text: Price and quantity are both indeterminate
options.feedback: Look again at quantity: both shifts push quantity up, so quantity rises for sure.

options.text: Quantity rises, but the change in price is indeterminate
options.feedback: Yes. Both shifts raise quantity. Demand pushes price up and supply pushes it down, so the price change depends on which shift is bigger.

options.text: Price rises and quantity rises
options.feedback: Demand shifting right pushes price up, but supply shifting right pushes price down. Without knowing the sizes, we cannot say price rises.

hints: Take one shift at a time: what does each do to price and to quantity?
When the two shifts push a variable the same way, we know its direction. When they push opposite ways, we do not.
check.worked: Example: in the market for apples, tastes move away from apples (demand left) and a storm destroys orchards (supply left). Both shifts lower quantity, so quantity falls. Demand left lowers price, supply left raises it, so the price change is indeterminate.
check.explanation: Demand right: price up, quantity up. Supply right: price down, quantity up. Together, quantity rises for sure, but the price could rise, fall or stay the same. It is **indeterminate** without knowing the size of each shift.

check.prompt: Beef and leather are in joint supply (both come from cattle). Demand for beef rises strongly. What happens in the **leather** market?

options.text: Demand for leather shifts right: leather price rises
options.feedback: Beef buyers do not need more leather. The link is on the production side, through the cattle.

options.text: Supply of leather shifts left: leather price rises
options.feedback: That would fit **competitive** supply, where goods compete for the same resources. In joint supply, more of one means more of the other.

options.text: Nothing changes in the leather market
options.feedback: Making more beef also makes more hides. That changes the supply of leather.

options.text: Supply of leather shifts right: leather price falls and quantity rises
options.feedback: Yes. Farmers raise more cattle for beef, which also produces more hides, so more leather is supplied at every price.

hints: What does making more beef also produce?
Joint supply: producing more of one good means producing more of the other.
check.worked: Example: demand for petrol rises, so refineries process more crude oil. This also produces more diesel, a jointly supplied good. Supply of diesel shifts right, so diesel's price falls.
check.explanation: In [[joint supply]], two goods come from one process. Higher beef demand raises beef output and so the number of hides. Leather supply shifts right: its price falls and quantity rises.

check.prompt: A smoothie stand market starts in equilibrium at $5. Then a heatwave raises demand. Use the schedule. At the **old price of $5**, what is the excess demand (shortage)?

mistakes.feedback: 70 is the new quantity demanded at $5. Excess demand is the **gap**: quantity demanded minus quantity supplied.
50 is the quantity supplied at $5 (and the old quantity demanded). Subtract it from the new quantity demanded.
There was no shortage **before** the heatwave. Use the quantity demanded **after** the heatwave.
Check the row: use the $5 row, not the new equilibrium at $6.

hints: Excess demand = quantity demanded minus quantity supplied, at one price.
Use the $5 row and the column for demand after the heatwave.
check.worked: Example with a different price: at $4 after the heatwave, quantity demanded is 80 and quantity supplied is 40. Excess demand = 80 − 40 = 40 smoothies.
check.explanation: At $5 after the heatwave: quantity demanded = 70 and quantity supplied = 50. Excess demand = 70 − 50 = **20 smoothies**. This shortage pushes the price up to the new equilibrium at $6, where 60 are bought and sold.

check.prompt: ^HL^ The price of strawberries falls and people buy more. Which explanation of the downward-sloping demand curve is correct?

options.text: Farmers supply more strawberries at a lower price
options.feedback: This is about sellers, and the law of supply says they supply **less** at a lower price. The question asks why buyers buy more.

options.text: Income effect: the same income now buys more. Substitution effect: strawberries are cheaper than other fruit, so people switch to them
options.feedback: Yes. Both effects make quantity demanded rise when price falls.

options.text: Diminishing marginal utility: each extra punnet gives more satisfaction, so people want more
options.feedback: Diminishing marginal utility says each extra unit gives **less** extra satisfaction. That is why people buy more only at a lower price.

options.text: The fall in price shifts demand to the right
options.feedback: A change in the good's own price causes a movement along the curve, not a shift.

hints: Think about two effects of a lower price: on what your money can buy, and on how the good compares with other goods.
One effect is about real income. The other is about switching from substitutes.
check.worked: Example: bus fares fall. A student's weekly pocket money now pays for more trips (income effect). The bus is now cheaper compared with a taxi, so some taxi trips become bus trips (substitution effect).
check.explanation: At HL, demand slopes down because of the **income effect**, the **substitution effect** and the law of **diminishing marginal utility**: each extra unit adds less satisfaction, so consumers buy more only if the price falls.

check.prompt: The diagram shows a market after one event. **Label it.** Choose what each letter shows.

diagram.title: A demand and supply diagram with four lettered parts
diagram.description: Two parallel downward-sloping lines and one upward-sloping line. Letter A is on the left downward line. Letter B is on the right downward line. Letter C is on the upward line. Letter D is where the right downward line meets the upward line.

slots.feedback: A is on the dashed downward-sloping line, the demand curve before the event.
B is on the solid downward-sloping line to the right. Demand has increased.
C is on the upward-sloping line. Supply slopes up because firms supply more at higher prices.
D is where the new demand curve meets supply: the new equilibrium price and quantity.

hints: Demand slopes down and supply slopes up.
Which demand curve is to the right? Where does that curve cross supply?
check.worked: Example: incomes rise and pizza is a normal good. Demand shifts right from D₁ to D₂. The new equilibrium is where D₂ crosses S, at a higher price and quantity.
check.explanation: Demand shifted **right** from D₁ to D₂. Supply did not move. The new equilibrium is where D₂ meets S: price rises from $5 to $6 and quantity rises from 50 to 60.

check.prompt: Sam drew this diagram for the event: **"The cost of coffee beans falls."** (The market is for roasted coffee.) What is wrong with it?

diagram.title: Sam's diagram
diagram.description: Sam drew a demand curve D₁ shifting left to D₂, with supply S unchanged.

options.text: Sam shifted demand. A fall in an input cost shifts **supply to the right**.
options.feedback: Yes. Cheaper inputs lower the cost of production, so firms supply more at every price. Demand does not change.

options.text: Demand is the right curve, but it should shift right
options.feedback: A cost of production is a determinant of supply, not demand. Buyers do not want more coffee because beans are cheaper for roasters.

options.text: Supply should shift left
options.feedback: Right curve, wrong direction. Lower costs mean firms can supply more at every price, so supply shifts right.

options.text: Nothing is wrong
options.feedback: Check which curve moved. Is the cost of an input a determinant of demand or of supply?

hints: Is the cost of an input a determinant of demand or of supply?
Lower costs make producing cheaper. What do firms do at every price?
check.worked: Example: the price of flour falls. Bakeries can make bread more cheaply, so they supply more bread at every price. The supply curve for bread shifts right. The demand curve for bread does not move.
check.explanation: The **cost of factors of production** is a non-price determinant of **supply**. When it falls, supply shifts **right**. The equilibrium price falls and the equilibrium quantity rises.

explain.prompt: Using a demand and supply diagram, explain how Riverton's market for coffee beans moves to a new equilibrium after the "Frost on the farms" scenario.
explain.facts:
- The market starts in equilibrium at **$5** and **50 bags** (ceteris paribus).
- **Frost on the farms:** a frost damages coffee farms abroad. Green coffee beans, the roasters' main raw material, now cost much more.
- After the frost, roasters supply **20 fewer bags** at every price.

| Price | Demand (D) | Supply before (S₁) | Supply after (S₂) |
|---|---|---|---|
| $5 | 50 | 50 | 30 |
| $6 | 40 | 60 | 40 |
| $7 | 30 | 70 | 50 |

steps.lead: The frost made green coffee beans, the roasters' main raw material, cost much more. This is

options.text: a change in the price of coffee beans, so roasters move along the supply curve.
options.why: The cost of an input changed, not the price of the good itself. A non-price determinant shifts the curve.

options.text: a change in tastes, a non-price determinant of demand.
options.why: Buyers want the same amount at each price. The frost changes what sellers can supply.

options.text: a change in the cost of factors of production, a non-price determinant of supply.
options.why: Raw materials are a cost of production. Higher costs affect sellers, so this is about supply.

options.text: left from S₁ to S₂: roasters supply 20 fewer bags at every price.
options.why: Each bag costs more to roast, so roasters offer less at every price.

options.text: right from S₁ to S₂, because roasters can charge more.
options.why: Higher costs mean firms supply less at every price, so supply shifts left.

options.text: left, and the demand curve shifts left too, because coffee is dearer.
options.why: A higher price causes a movement along the demand curve, not a shift of it.

steps.lead: At the old price of $5, quantity demanded is still 50 bags but quantity supplied falls to 30, so there is

options.text: a surplus of 20 bags, and the price falls.
options.why: Buyers want more than sellers offer. That is a shortage, not a surplus.

options.text: a shortage of 20 bags, and the price rises.
options.why: Excess demand of 50 − 30 = 20 bags pushes the price up.

options.text: a shortage of 30 bags, and the price stays at $5.
options.why: The shortage is the gap: 50 − 30 = 20 bags. And a shortage pushes the price up.

steps.lead: As the price rises, it rations the scarce beans:

options.text: buyers who are not willing or able to pay more cut back, so quantity demanded falls along D.
options.why: This is the rationing function. The beans go to the buyers who value them most.

options.text: the demand curve shifts left until the shortage is gone.
options.why: Demand does not shift. Buyers move up along the same demand curve.

options.text: the government decides which buyers get the beans.
options.why: In a free market the price does the rationing, not the government.

steps.lead: At the same time, the higher price gives roasters

options.text: a reason to shift the supply curve back to the right.
options.why: The supply curve stays at S₂. The price change causes a movement along it.

options.text: a reason to supply less, because their costs went up.
options.why: The cost rise already shifted supply left. Along S₂, a higher price raises quantity supplied.

options.text: an incentive to supply more, so they move up along S₂.
options.why: A higher price means more profit per bag, so quantity supplied rises along S₂.

steps.lead: The new equilibrium is where D meets S₂:

options.text: the price rises to $6 and the quantity rises to 60 bags.
options.why: That is what happens when demand shifts right. Here supply shifted left, so quantity falls.

options.text: the price rises from $5 to $6, and the quantity falls from 50 to 40 bags.
options.why: At $6, quantity demanded and quantity supplied (S₂) are both 40 bags.

options.text: the price rises to $7, and the quantity falls to 30 bags.
options.why: At $7, roasters supply 50 bags on S₂ but buyers want only 30. That is a surplus, not equilibrium.

explain.own: For example, describe your diagram: label the axes, D, S₁ and S₂, and mark the old and new equilibrium points.

teacherNotes: Play the scenarios as a whole-class prediction game: students hold up D or S and point left or right before you reveal. The 17 shift scenarios cover every non-price determinant of demand and supply in the guide (2.1, 2.2). Turn on trap mode to practise shift versus movement along a curve; trap scenarios alternate with shift scenarios. After each shift, the gap at the old price shows excess demand or excess supply before the price adjusts (2.3 price mechanism), followed by a signalling, incentive or rationing question. The HL challenge and Check it question 8 cover income and substitution effects and diminishing marginal utility (HL 2.1). onComplete fires after 5 scenarios. Check it question 5 covers simultaneous shifts with an indeterminate outcome.
